choices: Run two instances in one AZ behind an ALB
Spread instances across multiple AZs with an ALB and Auto Scaling
Move the instances to a single larger instance
Add a second region with manual DNS failover
evidence:
AZ-a power event 02:14-04:40.
All 4 instances were in AZ-a.
ALB had no healthy targets.
scenarios.hint: What survives when one AZ fails?
scenarios.prompt: Which design survives this failure?
scenarios.situation: A 2.5-hour AZ power event took down an entire application because all instances lived in the failed AZ.
scenarios.title: The AZ that took everything
scenarios.why: Multi-AZ deployment across independent Availability Zones with a load balancer and Auto Scaling keeps serving traffic when one AZ fails — the load balancer routes around unhealthy targets and Auto Scaling replaces capacity. Single-AZ designs, vertical scaling, and manual cross-region failover don't solve an AZ-level failure automatically.

choices: EBS snapshots copied manually each night
evidence:
RPO: 15 minutes. RTO: 1 hour.
Threat model: full region loss.
scenarios.hint: Which storage is regional by design and replicates asynchronously across regions?
scenarios.prompt: Which storage design meets the RPO and survives region loss?
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires surviving a full region loss with at most 15 minutes of data loss and 1-hour recovery.
scenarios.title: Surviving a region loss
scenarios.why: S3 with Cross-Region Replication asynchronously replicates objects to another region, surviving region loss with a low RPO. S3 is already regional (data is stored across AZs); EBS/EFS are AZ-scoped without replication, and manual snapshots can't meet a 15-minute RPO reliably.

choices: An SQS queue between the API and the workers
A larger worker fleet with no queue
evidence:
Flash sale: 50x normal traffic for 20 min.
Workers OOM'd; orders lost.
Traffic then flat for hours.
scenarios.hint: What absorbs a burst so nothing is lost when consumers can't keep up?
scenarios.prompt: Which pattern absorbs the burst without losing orders?
scenarios.situation: A flash sale sends 50x normal traffic for 20 minutes; synchronous workers are overwhelmed and orders are lost.
scenarios.title: Decoupling the flash sale
scenarios.why: An SQS queue decouples producers from consumers: the API accepts orders into a durable queue and workers drain it at their own pace — no orders lost during bursts. Synchronous calls couple failure modes; bigger fleets still can't handle arbitrary spikes without a buffer.

choices: A single NAT gateway in one AZ
Public IPs on every database instance
A NAT gateway in each AZ, databases in private subnets
An internet gateway attached to the private subnets
evidence:
DB tier: private subnets.
Need: outbound patches, no inbound.
AZ-a NAT gateway failed last month.
scenarios.hint: NAT gateways are AZ-scoped — what happens to private subnets in other AZs?
scenarios.prompt: Which design is both secure and resilient?
scenarios.situation: Database instances in private subnets need outbound internet for patches but no inbound access. Last month's single NAT gateway failure in AZ-a cut off patching.
scenarios.title: Outbound-only, in every AZ
scenarios.why: A NAT gateway per AZ keeps private subnets' outbound access working when one AZ fails, and private subnets with no public IPs block inbound internet. A single NAT gateway is a single point of failure; public IPs on databases expose them; internet gateways don't provide outbound-only semantics.

choices: An Elastic IP moved manually to a standby
Route 53 health checks with failover routing to a warm standby in another region
A bigger instance in the primary region
DNS TTL set to 24 hours for stability
evidence:
SLO: 99.9% monthly (~43 min downtime).
Current: single-region active-passive
with manual failover (2h RTO).
scenarios.hint: 43 minutes of budget versus a 2-hour manual failover — what closes the gap?
scenarios.prompt: Which approach brings RTO inside the error budget?
scenarios.situation: A single-region app with manual failover (2-hour RTO) can't meet its 99.9% SLO (~43 min/month downtime budget).
scenarios.title: Failover faster than the budget
scenarios.why: Route 53 health checks with failover routing detect the outage and shift DNS to a warm standby automatically, cutting RTO to minutes. Manual Elastic IP moves keep the 2-hour RTO; bigger instances don't help region failure; long TTLs slow failover instead of speeding it.

choices: Deploy with rolling updates behind the ALB, keeping old instances until new ones pass health checks
Deploy to all instances simultaneously at 3 AM
Take the ALB out of service during deploys
Deploy to a single instance and copy its disk to the others
evidence:
Last deploy: all instances replaced at once.
Bad build took the site down for 40 min.
Rollback required a full re-deploy.
scenarios.hint: What keeps serving traffic while the new version proves itself?
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment strategy prevents the next all-at-once outage?
scenarios.situation: A deploy replaced all instances simultaneously; a bad build caused a 40-minute outage with a painful rollback.
scenarios.title: Never deploy to everything at once
scenarios.why: Rolling updates (or blue/green) keep the old version serving behind the load balancer until new instances pass health checks, so a bad build never takes all capacity at once and rollback is instant. Simultaneous replacement maximizes blast radius; removing the ALB or disk-copying are fragile anti-patterns.

choices: Add more read replicas in the same AZ
ElastiCache for Redis in front of the database
Switch to a larger single database instance
evidence:
p99 latency: 2.1s (target: 200ms).
Query mix: 95% reads, same keys.
DB CPU: 88%.
scenarios.hint: 95% repeated reads — what serves those without touching the database?
scenarios.prompt: Which change hits the 200ms target?
scenarios.situation: p99 latency is 2.1s against a 200ms target; 95% of queries are repeated reads of the same keys and the database CPU is pegged.
scenarios.title: The 2-second p99
scenarios.why: ElastiCache (Redis) absorbs repeated reads in memory with sub-millisecond latency, collapsing both DB load and p99. Read replicas still query disk-backed engines per request; vertical scaling is costly and doesn't fix the repeated-read pattern; S3 isn't a low-latency cache.

evidence:
Need: route /api/* to microservices,
 host-based routing, path-based routing,
 L7 health checks.
scenarios.hint: Which load balancer understands HTTP paths and hostnames?
scenarios.prompt: Which load balancer fits?
scenarios.situation: Microservices need path-based and host-based routing with Layer 7 health checks.
scenarios.title: Routing by path and host
scenarios.why: The Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and supports path-based and host-based routing plus HTTP health checks. NLB is Layer 4 (no path awareness), Gateway LB is for virtual appliances, and CloudFront is a CDN, not a service router.

choices: CloudFront with the ALB as origin
An NLB in front of the ALB
evidence:
Users: 60% EU, 25% APAC, 15% US.
Origin: us-east-1 only.
APAC p99: 3.4s.
scenarios.hint: What brings static and cacheable content physically closer to users?
scenarios.prompt: Which addition cuts global latency?
scenarios.situation: Most users are far from the single-region origin; APAC p99 latency is 3.4 seconds.
scenarios.title: Closer to the user
scenarios.why: CloudFront caches content at edge locations near users, cutting latency for the 85% of traffic outside the origin region and offloading the origin. Bigger ALBs don't fix distance; NLB in front of ALB adds nothing for global users; Direct Connect serves offices, not public users.

evidence:
DB: 40k sustained IOPS needed.
Latency: sub-millisecond.
Data: replicated at the app layer.
scenarios.hint: Which volume type is built for sustained high IOPS with sub-ms latency?
scenarios.prompt: Which storage meets the I/O profile?
scenarios.situation: A database needs 40,000 sustained IOPS with sub-millisecond latency; the application already replicates data itself.
scenarios.title: 40k IOPS, sub-millisecond
scenarios.why: io2 volumes provide provisioned IOPS with sub-millisecond latency for I/O-intensive databases. gp3 can't sustain 40k IOPS cost-effectively, instance store is ephemeral (data lost on stop), and EFS is a file system with higher latency.

evidence:
Writes: 5k/sec steady, 50k/sec spikes.
Access: key-value lookups by ID.
Ops team: 1 person.
scenarios.hint: Key-value by ID, massive spikes, one ops person — which database scales without provisioning?
scenarios.prompt: Which database handles the spikes with minimal ops?
scenarios.situation: Key-value lookups by ID at 5k writes/sec steady with 50k/sec spikes, managed by a single ops person.
scenarios.title: Spikes without provisioning
scenarios.why: DynamoDB with on-demand capacity scales automatically to absorb 10x write spikes on key-value access with no capacity planning and no servers to manage. RDS Multi-AZ doesn't auto-scale writes; self-managed EC2 maximizes ops burden; Redshift is an analytics warehouse, not an OLTP store.

choices: Amazon EventBridge with rules routing to targets
Direct Lambda invocation from each service
evidence:
12 services need order events.
Some need all events; some need only
high-value orders. Fan-out required.
scenarios.hint: Which service routes events by content to many targets?
scenarios.prompt: Which eventing design fits?
scenarios.situation: Twelve services consume order events with different filtering needs; the architecture must fan out without point-to-point wiring.
scenarios.title: Fan-out without spaghetti
scenarios.why: EventBridge provides a serverless event bus with rules that filter and route events to many targets — decoupling producers from consumers. SQS is point-to-point, SNS fan-out lacks content-based routing richness, and direct Lambda invocation creates tight coupling.

choices: A private subnet with a VPC endpoint for the service
A public subnet with a security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0
A NAT gateway with an allow-all route
evidence:
Workload: private, no public IPs.
Must call AWS services.
Traffic must not cross the internet.
scenarios.hint: What did the private-subnet scenario in Cloud Practitioner use?
scenarios.prompt: Which network design satisfies the policy?
scenarios.situation: A private workload with no public IPs must call AWS services without traffic crossing the public internet.
scenarios.title: Private to the core
scenarios.why: VPC endpoints (gateway or interface) keep traffic to AWS services on the AWS network from private subnets. Public subnets with open security groups violate the no-public-IP policy; NAT gateways still traverse the internet; Direct Connect public VIFs are for on-premises hybrid access.

choices: AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation
A config file in the repo
S3 with a restrictive bucket policy
evidence:
DB password: hardcoded in 14 repos.
Rotation: manual, last done 2022.
scenarios.hint: Which service rotates credentials for you?
scenarios.prompt: Which approach fixes rotation and sprawl?
scenarios.situation: A database password is hardcoded across 14 repositories and hasn't been rotated since 2022.
scenarios.title: Fourteen copies of the password
scenarios.why: Secrets Manager centralizes secrets and supports automatic rotation for RDS and other databases, eliminating hardcoded sprawl. Environment variables and config files still leak; S3 is storage, not a secrets lifecycle service.

evidence:
Need: subnet-wide stateless guardrail
PLUS instance-level stateful rules.
scenarios.hint: One is stateless at the subnet, the other stateful at the instance — do they compete or combine?
scenarios.prompt: Which firewalling approach is correct?
scenarios.situation: The design calls for subnet-wide stateless guardrails plus instance-level stateful rules.
scenarios.title: Two firewalls, two jobs
scenarios.why: Security groups (stateful, attached to instances/ENIs) and NACLs (stateless, attached to subnets) are complementary layers: NACLs provide coarse subnet guardrails, security groups provide precise instance rules. They don't replace each other, and IAM governs API access, not packets.

choices: AWS KMS with customer managed keys and key policies
SSE-S3 only, keys managed by AWS
Client-side encryption with keys in the repo
No encryption — the VPC is private
evidence:
Regulated data in S3.
Need: key rotation, audit of key use,
separation of duties for key admins.
scenarios.hint: Which service gives you key policies, rotation, and CloudTrail-logged key use?
scenarios.prompt: Which key management design meets the requirements?
scenarios.situation: Regulated data in S3 needs key rotation, auditing of key usage, and separation of duties for key administrators.
scenarios.title: Who holds the keys?
scenarios.why: KMS with customer managed keys provides key policies (separation of duties), automatic rotation, and CloudTrail logging of every key use. SSE-S3 offers no key control or audit; client-side keys in a repo are a breach waiting to happen; a private VPC doesn't encrypt data at rest.

evidence:
SOC needs: threat intel + ML-based
detection of anomalous API calls
and compromised instances.
scenarios.hint: Which service is the threat-detection one, not the logging one?
scenarios.prompt: Which service provides the detection?
scenarios.situation: The SOC wants ML-based detection of anomalous API activity and potentially compromised instances, fed by threat intelligence.
scenarios.title: Eyes on the threat feed
scenarios.why: GuardDuty is the threat-detection service: it analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs with ML and threat intelligence. CloudTrail/Flow Logs/Config are data sources and recorders, not detectors.

choices: One account with IAM users for everything
Separate accounts per environment/workload under AWS Organizations with SCPs
evidence:
3 teams, dev/stage/prod.
Blast radius: one team's mistake took
down prod last quarter.
scenarios.hint: What is the strongest blast-radius boundary AWS offers?
scenarios.prompt: Which account structure prevents recurrence?
scenarios.situation: Three teams share one account; one team's mistake took down production last quarter.
scenarios.title: Blast radius: the whole company
scenarios.why: Separate accounts per environment/workload under AWS Organizations — with Service Control Policies as guardrails — make the account boundary the blast-radius boundary. A single account can't isolate failures; shared root is an anti-pattern; VPC peering doesn't create security boundaries.

choices: Spot Instances for the batch workers
Reserved Instances for the batch workers
evidence:
Nightly render jobs: 6h, stateless,
checkpoint every 10 min.
Interrupt tolerance: high.
scenarios.hint: Which pricing is up to 90% off for interruptible work?
scenarios.prompt: Which pricing model fits the batch workers?
scenarios.situation: Nightly stateless render jobs run 6 hours, checkpoint frequently, and tolerate interruption.
scenarios.title: Discounts for interruptible work
scenarios.why: Spot Instances offer deep discounts for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch rendering with checkpointing. On-Demand wastes the discount; Reserved Instances commit to capacity that batch doesn't need; Dedicated Hosts serve compliance, not cost.

choices: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for all logs
evidence:
2 PB of logs, access pattern unknown
and changing. Retrieval: occasional.
scenarios.hint: Unknown, changing access patterns — which class moves data automatically?
scenarios.prompt: Which storage class minimizes cost without manual policy tuning?
scenarios.situation: 2 PB of logs with unknown and changing access patterns; retrieval is occasional.
scenarios.title: Access patterns you can't predict
scenarios.why: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent/infrequent/archive tiers based on observed access — ideal when patterns are unknown or changing. Standard overpays for cold data; Glacier Instant Retrieval penalizes the occasional retrievals; EBS isn't object storage.

choices: Compute Savings Plans covering the steady baseline
evidence:
Web tier: 40 instances baseline 24/7.
Peaks: 120 instances, 4h/day.
scenarios.hint: Commit to the part that never changes; stay flexible on the rest.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most cost-effective commitment strategy?
scenarios.situation: A web tier runs 40 instances 24/7 with daily peaks to 120 instances for 4 hours.
scenarios.title: Commit to the baseline
scenarios.why: Compute Savings Plans on the steady 40-instance baseline capture commitment discounts where they're safe, while peaks stay On-Demand (or Spot) for flexibility. All On-Demand wastes the baseline discount; Spot is wrong for the always-on web tier; committing to peak capacity strands commitment during off-peak.

choices: Keep the NAT gateway and accept the cost
VPC endpoints for the AWS services the workloads call
evidence:
NAT Gateway data processing:
$3,800/mo. Traffic: 90% to S3
and DynamoDB.
scenarios.hint: 90% of the traffic never needs the internet at all — what bypasses the NAT?
scenarios.prompt: What cuts this bill?
scenarios.situation: NAT Gateway data-processing charges are $3,800/month; 90% of the traffic goes to S3 and DynamoDB.
scenarios.title: The $3,800 NAT bill
scenarios.why: VPC endpoints route S3/DynamoDB traffic privately, bypassing NAT Gateway data-processing charges entirely (gateway endpoints are free). NAT instances trade one cost for ops burden; public subnets break the security model; accepting the cost ignores the obvious fix.

choices: The region closest to users and data-residency needs, then optimize within it
The region with the most AZs
Multiple regions for a single-region app
evidence:
Users: EU. Data residency: EU required.
Proposal: run in us-east-1 to save 10%.
scenarios.hint: What constraint makes the 10% saving irrelevant?
scenarios.prompt: How should region selection work here?
scenarios.situation: EU users and EU data-residency requirements; someone proposes us-east-1 to save 10%.
scenarios.title: Cheap region, wrong continent
scenarios.why: Data residency is a hard constraint that overrides price differences, and latency to EU users also argues for an EU region. Region choice starts from compliance and latency, then cost-optimize within the chosen region. Multi-region for a single-region app adds cost, not savings.

evidence:
400 instances, avg CPU 8%.
Team can't review each one manually.
scenarios.hint: Which service uses ML on CloudWatch history to recommend sizes?
scenarios.prompt: What finds the rightsizing opportunities at scale?
scenarios.situation: 400 instances average 8% CPU; the team can't review each one manually.
scenarios.title: Rightsizing 400 instances
scenarios.why: Compute Optimizer analyzes CloudWatch metrics with ML and recommends optimal instance types/sizes — built for exactly this fleet-scale rightsizing. Manual guessing doesn't scale; scaling up worsens waste; disabling CloudWatch removes the data needed for any analysis.

evidence:
Video transcode: 45-90 min per file.
Queue-driven, containerized already.
scenarios.hint: Lambda caps at 15 minutes — what runs containers without servers and without that cap?
scenarios.prompt: Which compute option fits?
scenarios.situation: Containerized video transcoding jobs take 45–90 minutes each, driven by a queue.
scenarios.title: Longer than Lambda allows
scenarios.why: Fargate runs containers serverlessly with no 15-minute execution cap, fitting long batch jobs. Lambda's 15-minute timeout rules it out; EC2 works but reintroduces server management; bare metal is for specialized licensing/hardware needs.

choices: EC2 Auto Scaling with simple scaling
EC2 Auto Scaling with target tracking on ALB request count
A fixed fleet sized for peak
evidence:
Traffic: gradual ramps + sudden spikes.
Metric: requests per target.
Goal: keep ~1000 req/target.
scenarios.hint: Which policy continuously drives toward the target metric?
scenarios.prompt: Which scaling policy holds the target?
scenarios.situation: Traffic ramps gradually with sudden spikes; the goal is to hold ~1000 requests per target.
scenarios.title: Holding 1000 requests per target
scenarios.why: Target tracking policies continuously adjust capacity to keep the chosen metric (ALB request count per target) at the target value — ideal for a request-driven goal. Simple scaling reacts in steps, fixed fleets waste money, and scheduled scaling can't handle sudden spikes.

choices: An AMI built by EC2 Image Builder, instances in an Auto Scaling group
Golden image copied manually to each instance
User data that apt-gets everything at boot (20 min boot)
evidence:
Boot time: 22 min (installs at boot).
Scaling too slow for spikes.
scenarios.hint: What bakes the install into the image so boot is fast?
scenarios.prompt: What fixes the slow scaling?
scenarios.situation: Instances take 22 minutes to boot because they install everything via user data at launch.
scenarios.title: 22-minute boots
scenarios.why: Baking dependencies into an AMI (automated with EC2 Image Builder) makes launches fast and consistent; Auto Scaling then reacts quickly. Manual image copies don't scale; boot-time installs are the root cause; a single instance has no scaling at all.

choices: Private subnets with NAT + security groups allowing only needed ports
The default VPC with default security group
evidence:
Bastion hosts being phased out.
Need: admin access without public IPs.
scenarios.hint: Which AWS service gives browser/CLI shell access with no bastion and no public IP?
scenarios.prompt: Which access design is most secure and operable?
scenarios.situation: Bastion hosts are being phased out; admins need shell access without public IPs.
scenarios.title: Life after the bastion
scenarios.why: Systems Manager Session Manager provides audited shell access to private instances with no bastion hosts, no public IPs, and no open inbound ports — logged to CloudTrail/S3. Private subnets with NAT plus least-privilege security groups support it; public subnets and default-open groups are regressions.

choices: HPC cluster with EFA and placement groups
evidence:
CFD simulation: tightly coupled MPI.
Needs: microsecond inter-node latency.
scenarios.hint: Which combination is built for tightly-coupled MPI?
scenarios.prompt: Which compute design fits tightly-coupled MPI?
scenarios.situation: A CFD simulation uses tightly-coupled MPI and needs microsecond inter-node latency.
scenarios.title: Microseconds between nodes
scenarios.why: HPC workloads need cluster placement groups (instances physically close) plus Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) for low-latency, high-throughput networking. A single instance can't scale; Lambda/Fargate lack the networking and duration profile for tightly-coupled MPI.

evidence:
Team: 1 dev. App: standard Node.js web.
Want: deploy code, get URL, minimal ops.
scenarios.hint: Which service is 'upload code, get a managed environment'?
scenarios.prompt: Which option minimizes ops for a solo developer?
scenarios.situation: A solo developer wants to deploy a standard Node.js web app and get a URL with minimal operational work.
scenarios.title: Deploy code, get URL
scenarios.why: Elastic Beanstalk is the PaaS option: upload code, and it provisions and manages the underlying EC2, load balancing, and scaling. Self-managed EC2 maximizes ops; Lambda doesn't fit a traditional long-running web server model as simply; Lightsail is simpler but less integrated for managed app environments.

choices: Amazon Aurora with a reader endpoint
evidence:
Reads: 80k/sec, growing.
Writes: 200/sec.
Engine: PostgreSQL-compatible required.
scenarios.hint: Which managed Postgres-compatible engine scales reads horizontally?
scenarios.prompt: Which database design scales the reads?
scenarios.situation: 80k reads/sec and growing on a PostgreSQL-compatible engine; writes are modest.
scenarios.title: 80k reads a second
scenarios.why: Aurora's storage-decoupled architecture supports up to 15 read replicas behind a reader endpoint, scaling PostgreSQL/MySQL-compatible reads horizontally. Multi-AZ alone adds a standby, not read scale; DynamoDB isn't relational; Redshift is analytics.

evidence:
Regulator: financial records immutable
for 7 years, not even by admins.
scenarios.hint: Which S3 feature enforces write-once-read-many, even against admins?
scenarios.prompt: Which storage meets the immutability requirement?
scenarios.situation: Financial records must be immutable for 7 years — not deletable even by administrators.
scenarios.title: Immutable for seven years
scenarios.why: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces WORM: objects can't be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, until retention expires. Versioning alone doesn't prevent deletion; EBS snapshots can be deleted; Glacier without Object Lock is just cheap storage.

evidence:
ML training: 100k IOPS scratch,
sub-ms latency, data rebuilt from S3
each run. Ephemeral is fine.
scenarios.hint: Ephemeral, extreme IOPS, rebuilt from S3 — which storage is designed to be temporary?
scenarios.prompt: Which storage fits the scratch workload?
scenarios.situation: ML training needs 100k IOPS scratch space with sub-ms latency; data is rebuilt from S3 each run and ephemerality is fine.
scenarios.title: Scratch space at 100k IOPS
scenarios.why: Instance store provides physically-attached NVMe storage with extreme IOPS and sub-ms latency at no extra cost — ideal for ephemeral scratch rebuilt from durable S3. EFS/FSx add cost and network hops; EBS can't reach these IOPS levels per volume as cheaply for throwaway data.

evidence:
10M keys, microsecond reads,
10x traffic spikes, key-value only.
Durability required.
scenarios.hint: Microsecond key-value with durability — which managed NoSQL plus its cache?
scenarios.prompt: Which combination meets the profile?
scenarios.situation: 10M keys, microsecond reads, 10x spikes, key-value access, durability required.
scenarios.title: Microseconds at 10x spikes
scenarios.why: DynamoDB provides durable managed key-value storage that scales to spikes, and DAX adds a microsecond in-memory cache in front. RDS replicas are relational overhead for key-value; cache-only loses durability; Aurora Serverless v1 pauses and has scaling latency unsuited to 10x spikes.

evidence:
Fraud detection: 6-hop traversals
over account/transaction graph.
Relational JOINs timing out.
scenarios.hint: Multi-hop traversals over relationships — which database is built for graphs?
scenarios.prompt: Which database fits the traversal workload?
scenarios.situation: Fraud detection needs 6-hop traversals over an account/transaction graph; relational JOINs time out.
scenarios.title: Six hops, no JOINs
scenarios.why: Neptune is the purpose-built graph database for multi-hop traversals over highly connected data. Relational JOINs explode combinatorially on graph traversals; DynamoDB is key-value; MemoryDB is a Redis-compatible cache, not a graph engine.

evidence:
200 volumes. Policy: daily snaps,
retain 30 days. Current: manual,
missed 40% of days.
scenarios.hint: Which service automates snapshot lifecycles by policy?
scenarios.prompt: What automates the snapshot policy?
scenarios.situation: 200 EBS volumes need daily snapshots with 30-day retention; manual snapshots miss 40% of days.
scenarios.title: Snapshots on autopilot
scenarios.why: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates EBS snapshot creation, retention, and deletion by policy — eliminating the missed manual snapshots. Snapshots already go to S3 under the hood; cross-AZ replication isn't an EBS feature; manual processes are the current failure.

lessons.title: Resilient Architectures — Core concepts
concepts: Multi-AZ deployment across independent Availability Zones with a load balancer and Auto Scaling keeps serving traffic when one AZ fails — the load balancer routes around unhealthy targets and Auto Scaling replaces capacity.
SQS: an SQS queue decouples producers from consumers: the API accepts orders into a durable queue and workers drain it at their own pace — no orders lost during bursts.
Principle: single-AZ designs, vertical scaling, and manual cross-region failover don't solve an AZ-level failure automatically.

lessons.title: Secure Architectures — Core concepts
concepts: VPC endpoints (gateway or interface) keep traffic to AWS services on the AWS network from private subnets. SSE-S3 offers no key control or audit; client-side keys in a repo are a breach waiting to happen; a private VPC doesn't encrypt data at rest.
Secrets Manager centralizes secrets and supports automatic rotation for RDS and other databases, eliminating hardcoded sprawl.

Security groups (stateful, attached to instances/ENIs) and NACLs (stateless, attached to subnets) are complementary layers: NACLs provide coarse subnet guardrails, security groups provide precise instance rules.
KMS with customer managed keys provides key policies (separation of duties), automatic rotation, and CloudTrail logging of every key use.

example.code:
DB password: hardcoded in 14 repos.
Rotation: manual, last done 2022.
example.walkthrough: Secrets Manager centralizes secrets and supports automatic rotation for RDS and other databases, eliminating hardcoded sprawl. Environment variables and config files still leak; S3 is storage, not a secrets lifecycle service.

pitfalls: Common trap: security groups (stateful, instance-level).
Common trap: a public subnet with a security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0.
Common trap: store secrets in environment variables.
Common trap: client-side encryption with keys in the repo.

lessons.title: Cost-Optimized Architectures — Core concepts
concepts: Spot Instances offer deep discounts for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch rendering with checkpointing. Compute Savings Plans on the steady 40-instance baseline capture commitment discounts where they're safe, while peaks stay On-Demand (or Spot) for flexibility.

Cost optimization: NAT instances trade one cost for ops burden; public subnets break the security model; accepting the cost ignores the obvious fix. Multi-region for a single-region app adds cost, not savings.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent/infrequent/archive tiers based on observed access — ideal when patterns are unknown or changing.
Baseline vs peak: all On-Demand wastes the baseline discount; Spot is wrong for the always-on web tier; committing to peak capacity strands commitment during off-peak.
NAT gateway costs: VPC endpoints route S3/DynamoDB traffic privately, bypassing NAT Gateway data-processing charges entirely (gateway endpoints are free).

example.code:
Web tier: 40 instances baseline 24/7.
Peaks: 120 instances, 4h/day.
example.walkthrough: Compute Savings Plans on the steady 40-instance baseline capture commitment discounts where they're safe, while peaks stay On-Demand (or Spot) for flexibility. All On-Demand wastes the baseline discount; Spot is wrong for the always-on web tier; committing to peak capacity strands commitment during off-peak.

pitfalls: Common trap: savings Plans covering peak capacity.
Common trap: keep the NAT gateway and accept the cost.
Common trap: VPC endpoints for the AWS services the workloads call.
Common trap: reserved Instances for the batch workers.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Compute — Core concepts
concepts: Fargate runs containers serverlessly with no 15-minute execution cap, fitting long batch jobs. A single instance can't scale; Lambda/Fargate lack the networking and duration profile for tightly-coupled MPI.

Lambda's 15-minute timeout rules it out; EC2 works but reintroduces server management; bare metal is for specialized licensing/hardware needs. Self-managed EC2 maximizes ops; Lambda doesn't fit a traditional long-running web server model as simply; Lightsail is simpler but less integrated for managed app environments.

Auto Scaling policies: baking dependencies into an AMI (automated with EC2 Image Builder) makes launches fast and consistent; Auto Scaling then reacts quickly. Target tracking policies continuously adjust capacity to keep the chosen metric (ALB request count per target) at the target value — ideal for a request-driven goal.
Image Builder: manual image copies don't scale; boot-time installs are the root cause; a single instance has no scaling at all.
Systems Manager Session Manager provides audited shell access to private instances with no bastion hosts, no public IPs, and no open inbound ports — logged to CloudTrail/S3.

example.code:
Video transcode: 45-90 min per file.
Queue-driven, containerized already.
example.walkthrough: Fargate runs containers serverlessly with no 15-minute execution cap, fitting long batch jobs. Lambda's 15-minute timeout rules it out; EC2 works but reintroduces server management; bare metal is for specialized licensing/hardware needs.

pitfalls: Common trap: EC2 Auto Scaling with simple scaling.
Common trap: private subnets with NAT + security groups allowing only needed ports.
Common trap: golden image copied manually to each instance.
Common trap: user data that apt-gets everything at boot (20 min boot).
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: Storage & Database — Core concepts
concepts: Aurora's storage-decoupled architecture supports up to 15 read replicas behind a reader endpoint, scaling PostgreSQL/MySQL-compatible reads horizontally. RDS replicas are relational overhead for key-value; cache-only loses durability; Aurora Serverless v1 pauses and has scaling latency unsuited to 10x spikes.
Read scaling: multi-AZ alone adds a standby, not read scale; DynamoDB isn't relational; Redshift is analytics.
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces WORM: objects can't be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, until retention expires.
Instance store provides physically-attached NVMe storage with extreme IOPS and sub-ms latency at no extra cost — ideal for ephemeral scratch rebuilt from durable S3.
Ephemeral storage: dynamoDB provides durable managed key-value storage that scales to spikes, and DAX adds a microsecond in-memory cache in front.

example.code:
Regulator: financial records immutable
for 7 years, not even by admins.
example.walkthrough: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces WORM: objects can't be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, until retention expires. Versioning alone doesn't prevent deletion; EBS snapshots can be deleted; Glacier without Object Lock is just cheap storage.

pitfalls: Common trap: amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) policies.
Common trap: glacier Deep Archive without lock.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Terminal tab →

lessons.title: AWS Solutions Architect — Core concepts
concepts: Design VPCs in tiers: public subnets hold only internet-facing entry points (load balancers), private subnets hold app and data tiers, and NAT gateways per AZ give private resources safe outbound access. Security groups (stateful, instance-level) beat NACLs (stateless, subnet-level) for most filtering.

Build for AZ failure, not instance failure: load balancers and Auto Scaling groups span AZs, RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby, and S3 is AZ-redundant by default. If one building can take you down, the design is incomplete.

Choose the load balancer by protocol: ALB for HTTP/HTTPS with content-based routing, NLB for TCP/UDP with static IPs and extreme performance, GWLB for inserting network appliances. There is no universal balancer.

Tier S3 storage to access patterns with lifecycle policies — Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, and the Glacier family trade retrieval speed for price. Paying Standard rates for data you never read is the most common storage waste.

Pick data stores by access pattern: RDS/Aurora when you need SQL, joins, and transactions; DynamoDB when you need key-value scale at single-digit milliseconds; Redshift for analytics; ElastiCache to shed read load. One database rarely serves every pattern well.
Decouple with queues and events: SQS buffers work between tiers, SNS/EventBridge fan out notifications, and async boundaries let each tier scale and fail independently.

example.walkthrough: Inspecting route tables shows which subnets are truly public (a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an Internet Gateway) versus private. Architects verify this before trusting any diagram — a 'private' subnet with an IGW route is public.

pitfalls: Common trap: one NAT gateway per VPC — if its AZ fails, every private subnet loses outbound access; use one per AZ.
Common trap: enabling S3 Cross-Region Replication and calling it a backup — replication copies objects, it does not protect against deletion without versioning and Object Lock.
Common trap: ALB for non-HTTP workloads — ALB only speaks Layer 7; TCP/UDP services need NLB.
Common trap: designing single-AZ 'to save money' while the business cannot tolerate the resulting downtime window.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

foundations.why_needed: Architecting on AWS means designing VPCs, subnets, DNS, and load balancing. This track teaches the networking those designs assume.
EC2 administration and troubleshooting happen over SSH on Linux. Learn the command line before the ops scenarios.
Secure architectures are IAM architectures. Learn users, roles, and policies before designing access.

simulations.title: The instance that went dark
simulations.brief: Monday 09:12: monitoring pages — ilb-web-01 stopped responding to health checks, but the instance state is 'running'. Diagnose in order; every wrong click costs the team minutes.

steps.symptom: Health checks fail for ilb-web-01; instance state is 'running'.
options: Reboot the instance — it is probably a hung OS
Check the security group and NACL rules for the health-check path
Terminate and relaunch — fastest way to get a fresh host
Increase the instance type — t3.medium must be undersized
steps.explain: A running instance failing health checks points at the network path first: security groups, NACLs, route tables. Rebooting or resizing before checking the boundary wastes the investigation.

steps.symptom: Security group ilb-web-sg allows 443 from the load balancer; NACLs are default-allow.
options: The app must be down — restart the application tier
Check whether the app is listening on 443 inside the instance
Add 0.0.0.0/0 to the security group to rule out networking
Fail over to us-east-1b — the AZ must be impaired
steps.explain: With the boundary verified, the next layer is the workload itself: is the process listening? Opening the SG to the world or failing over the AZ skips the actual diagnosis.

simulations.debrief: You worked the classic layered diagnosis: instance state, then network boundary, then workload. That order is the SAA troubleshooting reflex.

simulations.title: Design the checkout tier
simulations.brief: You are the architect for a checkout service that must survive an AZ failure with no data loss. Each design decision compounds — choose the resilient path.

steps.text: Where do you place the application servers?

choices.label: One AZ — simpler and cheaper
choices.feedback: A single AZ is a single point of failure. The requirement says survive an AZ loss.

choices.label: Across two AZs behind a load balancer
choices.feedback: Correct — multi-AZ placement with a load balancer is the baseline resilient pattern.

steps.text: The reviewer rejects single-AZ. Reconsider: where do the app servers go?

choices.label: Across two AZs behind a load balancer
choices.feedback: Right. Cost savings never justify violating the stated resilience requirement.

steps.text: The database: which option meets 'no data loss' across an AZ failure?

choices.label: Single-AZ RDS with daily snapshots
choices.feedback: Daily snapshots mean up to 24h of data loss — that fails the requirement.

choices.label: Multi-AZ RDS with automated failover
choices.feedback: Correct — synchronous standby replication gives automatic failover with no data loss.

simulations.debrief: You designed for the stated requirement, not the cheapest bill: multi-AZ compute behind a load balancer, Multi-AZ database for zero data loss.

simulations.title: Stand up the three-tier app

steps.context: Deploy a three-tier app: network, security, data, compute, traffic.
items: Launch EC2 instances into the private subnets
Create the VPC with public and private subnets across two AZs
Attach the Application Load Balancer and register targets
Create security groups for ALB, app, and database tiers

simulations.debrief: You built bottom-up: network, then security boundaries, then data, then compute, then traffic. Foundations first is the architect's ordering instinct.

simulations.title: The wide-open database
simulations.brief: A peer asks you to review these security group rules before the database goes live. Click the lines that would fail a secure-architecture review.

steps.config:
sg-ilb-db-sg inbound:
1. 5432/tcp from 10.0.2.0/24 (app tier)
2. 22/tcp from 0.0.0.0/0 (admin SSH)
3. 5432/tcp from 0.0.0.0/0 (app access)
4. all traffic from sg-ilb-app-sg

issues.description: SSH open to the entire internet invites brute-force attacks against the database host.
issues.fix: Restrict 22/tcp to a bastion host or admin CIDR, or remove SSH and use Session Manager.

issues.description: Database port open to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes Postgres to the whole internet.
issues.fix: Allow 5432 only from the application tier (line 1 already covers it) and delete this rule.

simulations.debrief: You caught the two internet-wide openings on a database host. Line 1 and line 4 are the correct least-privilege patterns — keep those.

sections.heading: Resilient Architectures
items: Multi-AZ — Multi-AZ deployment across independent Availability Zones with a load balancer and Auto Scaling keeps serving traffic when one AZ fails — the load balancer routes around unhealthy targets and Auto Scaling replaces capacity.
SQS — an SQS queue decouples producers from consumers: the API accepts orders into a durable queue and workers drain it at their own pace — no orders lost during bursts.
Principle — single-AZ designs, vertical scaling, and manual cross-region failover don't solve an AZ-level failure automatically.
Common trap — add a second region with manual DNS failover.
Common trap — a NAT gateway in each AZ, databases in private subnets.
Common trap — a single NAT gateway in one AZ.
Common trap — DNS TTL set to 24 hours for stability.

S3 — S3 with Cross-Region Replication asynchronously replicates objects to another region, surviving region loss with a low RPO. S3 is already regional (data is stored across AZs); EBS/EFS are AZ-scoped without replication, and manual snapshots can't meet a 15-m…

sections.heading: High-Performing Architectures
items: ElastiCache — ElastiCache (Redis) absorbs repeated reads in memory with sub-millisecond latency, collapsing both DB load and p99.
ALB — bigger ALBs don't fix distance; NLB in front of ALB adds nothing for global users; Direct Connect serves offices, not public users.
CDN — NLB is Layer 4 (no path awareness), Gateway LB is for virtual appliances, and CloudFront is a CDN, not a service router.
CloudFront — CloudFront caches content at edge locations near users, cutting latency for the 85% of traffic outside the origin region and offloading the origin.
Common trap — EBS gp3 with default settings.
Common trap — EBS io2 with provisioned IOPS.
Common trap — switch to a larger single database instance.
Common trap — direct Connect for end users.

sections.heading: Secure Architectures
items: VPC — VPC endpoints (gateway or interface) keep traffic to AWS services on the AWS network from private subnets. SSE-S3 offers no key control or audit; client-side keys in a repo are a breach waiting to happen; a private VPC doesn't encrypt data at rest.
Secrets Manager centralizes secrets and — supports automatic rotation for RDS and other databases, eliminating hardcoded sprawl.

Security — Security groups (stateful, attached to instances/ENIs) and NACLs (stateless, attached to subnets) are complementary layers: NACLs provide coarse subnet guardrails, security groups provide precise instance rules.
KMS with customer managed keys — provides key policies (separation of duties), automatic rotation, and CloudTrail logging of every key use.
Common trap — security groups (stateful, instance-level).
Common trap — a public subnet with a security group allowing 0.0.0.0/0.
Common trap — store secrets in environment variables.
Common trap — client-side encryption with keys in the repo.

Secrets Manager centralizes secrets and — supports automatic rotation for RDS and other databases, eliminating hardcoded sprawl. Environment variables and config files still leak; S3 is storage, not a secrets lifecycle service.

sections.heading: Cost-Optimized Architectures
items: Spot Instances — Spot Instances offer deep discounts for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch rendering with checkpointing. Compute Savings Plans on the steady 40-instance baseline capture commitment discounts where they're safe, while peaks stay On-Demand (or…

Cost optimization — NAT instances trade one cost for ops burden; public subnets break the security model; accepting the cost ignores the obvious fix. Multi-region for a single-region app adds cost, not savings.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering — S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent/infrequent/archive tiers based on observed access — ideal when patterns are unknown or changing.
Baseline vs peak — all On-Demand wastes the baseline discount; Spot is wrong for the always-on web tier; committing to peak capacity strands commitment during off-peak.
NAT gateway costs — VPC endpoints route S3/DynamoDB traffic privately, bypassing NAT Gateway data-processing charges entirely (gateway endpoints are free).
Common trap — savings Plans covering peak capacity.
Common trap — keep the NAT gateway and accept the cost.
Common trap — VPC endpoints for the AWS services the workloads call.
Common trap — reserved Instances for the batch workers.

Compute Savings Plans — Compute Savings Plans on the steady 40-instance baseline capture commitment discounts where they're safe, while peaks stay On-Demand (or Spot) for flexibility. All On-Demand wastes the baseline discount; Spot is wrong for the always-on web tier; committing…

sections.heading: Compute
items: Fargate — Fargate runs containers serverlessly with no 15-minute execution cap, fitting long batch jobs. A single instance can't scale; Lambda/Fargate lack the networking and duration profile for tightly-coupled MPI.

Lambda — Lambda's 15-minute timeout rules it out; EC2 works but reintroduces server management; bare metal is for specialized licensing/hardware needs. Self-managed EC2 maximizes ops; Lambda doesn't fit a traditional long-running web server model as simply; Lightsai…

Auto Scaling policies — baking dependencies into an AMI (automated with EC2 Image Builder) makes launches fast and consistent; Auto Scaling then reacts quickly. Target tracking policies continuously adjust capacity to keep the chosen metric (ALB request count per target) at the ta…
Image Builder — manual image copies don't scale; boot-time installs are the root cause; a single instance has no scaling at all.
Systems Manager Session Manager — provides audited shell access to private instances with no bastion hosts, no public IPs, and no open inbound ports — logged to CloudTrail/S3.
Common trap — EC2 Auto Scaling with simple scaling.
Common trap — private subnets with NAT + security groups allowing only needed ports.
Common trap — golden image copied manually to each instance.
Common trap — user data that apt-gets everything at boot (20 min boot).

sections.heading: Storage & Database
items: Aurora's storage-decoupled architecture — supports up to 15 read replicas behind a reader endpoint, scaling PostgreSQL/MySQL-compatible reads horizontally. RDS replicas are relational overhead for key-value; cache-only loses durability; Aurora Serverless v1 pauses and has scaling latency unsuited t…
Read scaling — multi-AZ alone adds a standby, not read scale; DynamoDB isn't relational; Redshift is analytics.
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces WORM — objects can't be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, until retention expires.
Instance store — provides physically-attached NVMe storage with extreme IOPS and sub-ms latency at no extra cost — ideal for ephemeral scratch rebuilt from durable S3.
Ephemeral storage — dynamoDB provides durable managed key-value storage that scales to spikes, and DAX adds a microsecond in-memory cache in front.
Common trap — amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) policies.
Common trap — glacier Deep Archive without lock.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Resilient Architectures: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one High-Performing Architectures lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Secure Architectures terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
